newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon holds final round of election.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon holds final round of election.

text.p: Lebanese in the eastern Bekaa valley vote on Sunday in the final round of elections that have already returned an overwhelming majority of pro-Syrian deputies to parliament.
Polling stations open at 7.00 a.m. (0400 GMT) and close at 5.00 p.m. (1400 GMT).
The Bekaa's 410,000 voters will elect 23 deputies to the 128-member parliament in the fifth round of regional voting that began on August 18. Results are expected on Monday or Tuesday.
A 23-man pro-government list, including six ministers, several deputies and candidates of Hizbollah and Amal, Lebanon's two main Shi'ite Moslem movements, is expected to win.
It is challenged by two other tickets, including a 10-man list of leftists headed by communist party chief Farouk Dahrouje.
Newspapers said the opposition candidate most likely to win a seat was Tarek Habchi, a popular Maronite Christian representing the town of Zahle on the leftist list.

Habchi could benefit from indignation among Bekaa Christians that under a Syrian-brokered deal the Maronite on the government list for Zahle was chosen by Hizbollah, a pro-Iranian Shi'ite Moslem group. He is a nephew of President Elias Hrawi.

Syria, which has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and a strong presence in the Bekaa, played the major role in forming the pro-government list and also tried to mould the opposition tickets, political analysts said.

Syrian liaison officers politely told Bekaa politicians who was acceptable and who was not acceptable on their lists, political sources in the region said. Some politicians who had offended the Syrians were excludled from all three lists.
The resulting pro-government list is a disparate group of political rivals, pressed to run together to avert an electoral battle in the Bekaa, analysts said.
The main rivals are Hizbollah (Party of God) and the secular Amal movement which were also pressed onto a joint list in last week's vote in south Lebanon.
Hizbollah and Amal are rivals for leadership of the 1.3 million Shi'ite Moslem community and fought a sporadic war in the late 1980s.
Hizbollah has three members and two supporters on the goverment list. If all win, it will have seven deputies and two allies in the new parliament compared with eight deputies and four allies before.
